form: Variation in the ʔayʔaǰuθəm determiner system* Rachel Kelly, Marianne Huijsmans, and Mary McCarthy1  University of Alberta Abstract: Reisinger, Huijsmans & Matthewson (2021) describe an ʔayʔaǰuθəm determiner paradigm centred on the presence of current or previous direct evidence ( tə and šɛ) for the referent of the noun phrase or absence of direct evidence (kʷ). Further investigation suggests many speakers omit the šɛ determiner, instead presenting a two -determiner system (tə and kʷ). In this study, three of these speakers were presented with a series of contexts differing in the availability and timing of direct evidence for a target referent. We hypothesized these speakers would continue to use kʷ in evidence neutral contexts, but the tə determiner would shift to replace šɛ in instances of previous direct evidence. Our findings confirm the ongoing use of kʷ in evidence neutral contexts and the diminishing use of šɛ in favour of tə across direct evidence contexts. We further posit that various language internal factors motivate this shift rather than pressure from English. Keywords: ʔayʔaǰuθəm, evidentiality, determiners, semantics, variation

form: In this paper, we provide an update on the determiner system in ʔayʔaǰuθəm, following up on earlier work by Reisinger, Huijsmans, & Matthewson (2021). Determiners are grammatical markers that precede nouns, such as the and a in English. In ʔayʔaǰuθəm, the choice between determiners depends on whether the speaker sees the referent of the noun phrase at the time of speaking or previously saw the referent of the noun phrase. In the case of nonvisible referents, the distinction is whether the speaker has or had a direct experience of the referent through other senses. More specifically, Reisinger, Huijsmans, & Matthewson (2021) describe a system with three main determiners: tə is used when the speaker perceives the referent at the time of speaking, šɛ is used when the speaker perceived the referent previously, and kʷ is used when speaking of things that the speaker has never perceived. However, more recent work has shown that the determiner system varies between speakers, with many speakers rarely or never using šɛ. Our purpose here is to document and analyze the determiner system of these speakers.

form: We find, using a picture -prompt methodology, that this alternative system is organized very similarly to the one described in Reisinger, Huijsmans, and Matthewson (2021), except that tə is used both in cases where the speaker previously saw the referent and when it is currently in view. We propose that tə has generalized to encode that the speaker has direct evidence for the referent (or perhaps more specifically direct visual evidence; see Section 4) , while šɛ is falling out of use. The gradual loss of šɛ is likely due to language -internal pressures, as determiners are frequently elided (e.g., Kroeber 1991:91–92, 171–172; Watanabe 2003:379), which we hypothesize is leading gradually to the disappearance of less commonly used determiners in the paradigm. Th e more specialized (and therefore even less frequently used) feminine singular determiners have already almost entirely fallen out of use. Both varieties of the determiner system are organized according to principles different from those of English, so the difference between them is not due to English influence.

who: Rachel Kelly, Marianne Huijsmans and Mary McCarthy
form: Understanding the two systems is important in the context of ongoing language reclamation efforts, since learners and teachers need to navigate this variation. Learners will likely want to focus on the variety they hear in their own family or with the speakers they interact with most, and it will be useful for teachers to be able to guide them in this learning. A major aim of this paper is therefore to support learners and teachers engaged in teaching and learning the intricacies of the determiner system. We also anticipate the findings being of interest to linguists interested in the meaning of determiners and linguistic variation.

form: ʔayʔaǰuθəm is a Central Salish language traditionally spoken by members Tla’amin, Homalco, Klahoose, and K’ómoks First Nations, whose traditional territories span the northern Georgia Strait in British Columbia. A report from the First Nations Peoples’ Cu ltural Council (2018) indicates that there are only 47 native speakers, all aged 60 and above. More recently, they report that fluent speakers make up 3% of the population of these four communities, while 9% are learners (First Nations Peoples Cultural Council, 2022). There are strong language reclamation efforts underway in the four sister nations, including immersion programming for K -Gr.1 in Tla’amin and an adult university-level proficiency program offered in partnership with the University of Victoria. While the language is mutually intelligible between the four nations, there are dialect differences. The biggest difference lies between the island dialect, spoken previously by members of the K’ómoks Nation, and the dialects spoken in the remaining three nations, collectively known as the mainland variety. However, no mother tongue speakers are remaining in K’ómoks. The dialect differences between Tla’amin, Homalco, and Klahoose are more subtle, and the dialect boundaries are somewhat obscured by intermarriage and the close family ties between the nations, so that it is not always clear what is a dialect difference and what is a familylect. Reisinger, Huijsmans, & Matthewson’s (2021) previous analysis of the ʔayʔaǰuθəm determiner system was based on close work with Tla’amin Elder qaʔaχstalɛs (Dr. Elsie Paul), and corroborative evidence from several additional speakers from Tla’amin and Homal co, including Ochele (Betty Wilson) and the late Marion Harry. For the current paper, we worked especially closely with Molly Harry from Homalco, with corroborative evidence from several additional speakers from Homalco and Tla’amin, Doreen Point and the late Freddie Louie.

form: Reisinger, Huijsmans, and Matthewson (2021) reframed the semantic distribution of the kʷ, tə, and šɛ determiners with the primary distinction cent ering on the presence versus the absence of direct evidence. Direct evidence is defined as any source of evidence that confirms the existence of an entity to the speaker without requiring them to make any further inference. For instance, seeing a bear is direct evidence for the bear, but seeing a bear’s footprints is indirect evidence, since one infers based on the footprints that a bear was present.

who: Rachel Kelly, Marianne Huijsmans and Mary McCarthy
form: Within the category of direct evidence, there is a further divide between the Current Direct Evidence (CDE) and Previous Direct Evidence (PDE) . When the referent is perceived at the time of speaking, the speaker has CDE for the referent, and the tə determiner is used. On the other hand, when the referent was perceived before the time of speaking but is no longer, the speaker has PDE, and the šɛ determiner is selected. When the speaker has no direct evidence for the thing described by the noun phrase (neither current nor prior), they select the Evidence Neutral form kʷ. The organization of the determiners according to these evidential distinctions is shown in Table 1.

form: Our picture stimuli were designed to elicit target nouns across the three semantic contexts: 1) contexts where the speaker has CDE for the entity described by the target noun phrase, 2) contexts where the speaker of the utterance has PDE for the entity described by the target noun phrase, and 3) contexts where the speaker has indirect evidence for the entity described by the target noun phrase or no evidence for what is described by the target noun phrase (EvN contexts). The picture prompts for our main task were designed using Canva, which allowed the high degree of customization needed to portray the necessary relationships, thoughts, and feelings required to illustrate the context. Alongside each picture prompt, a brief verbal narrative of each photo was given to help establish the context. Then, the language consultant was provided with an English phrase and was asked to translate this into ʔayʔaǰuθəm. While the three semantic categories were generally introduced following a fixed sequence from CDE and PDE to EvN, the order was occasionally reversed (EvN –PDE–CDE) to check that the order did not affect the speaker’s determiner choice. Table 2 depicts example stimuli using the target noun kʷaʔəmnač ‘roots’ across the three semantic contexts, including the corresponding narrative and English prompt for each condition.

who: Rachel Kelly, Marianne Huijsmans and Mary McCarthy
form: The main task was completed over many elicitation sessions spanning March 2025 —June 2025. We presented 92 target contexts. While we initially aimed for an even balance across contexts, seven of the contexts intended as EvN contexts were reclassified as PDE contexts. These contexts were intended to involve the speaker having only reported information for the target entity; however, in delivering the context, the researchers mistakenly targeted only the utterance from the individual who did see the target entity.

form: Determiners in the PDE category are mixed, counter to the hypothesis that tə is used for all entities for which the speaker has direct evidence (both those seen/experienced now and previously seen/experienced). form: We hypothesize that the frequent elision of determiners in everyday speech has created an avenue internal to the language for the loss of less -frequent members of the paradigm. The first determiners to disappear are the feminine singular determiners, which have quite a narrow distribution and are sometimes replaced by the gender/number neutral counterparts, even in the speech of the oldest speaker we work with. šɛ seems to be in the process of disappearing now for many speakers. As šɛ falls out of use, tə is becoming a determiner used generally for all entities for which the speaker has visual evidence.

form: This characterization of the relationship between the two determiner systems is one of language change, rather than dialect variation. This is desirable, as there is no clear dialect division among the speakers using the two systems. We have worked with Tla’amin and Homalco speakers who use šɛ regularly as a core part of the paradigm and with Tla’amin and Homalco speakers who rarely or never use šɛ. The determiner šɛ is also found in early records of the language from Boas’s work in the 1890s (along with the feminine singular determiners), so the trajectory does seem to be one of determiner loss rather than innovation.8 The proposal that determiner elision is contributing to the loss of less frequent forms relies on šɛ being less frequent than tə, even for those speakers who use it as a core element of their paradigm. Checking whether this is true of natural speech is difficult. In traditional narratives, speakers tend to shift perspective as if they are viewing the scenes and use the tə determiner even for entities they do not see in the actual speech situation (Huijsmans, Reisinger, & Matthewson, 20 20:173, fn. 8). Personal narratives are better suited to this investigation, but there are not many fully transcribed and glossed that we have access to. However, Watanabe (2025) is a lovely personal narrative from Mrs. Mary George about blackberry picking she had done earlier in the morning, before recording. In it, we find 10 instances of šɛ and 21 of tə. In one conversation we have fully transcribed between qaʔaχstalɛs (Dr. Elsie Paul) and Molly Harry, we find that qaʔaχstalɛs uses šɛ 3 times and tə 10 times. These very preliminary counts are consistent with tə occurring more frequently than šɛ, but further investigation is needed.

form: If Table 4 accurately represents the alternate determiner system, it raises an interesting question concerning competition between the forms in the paradigm. Usually, when a speaker has a choice between paradigmatic alternatives, and one is more informativ e and still fits the context, that alternative will be preferred. For instance, Heim (1991) analyzes the choice between English determiners in terms of Maximize Presupposition. In her analysis, the definite determiner presupposes a unique individual matching the NP description in the context, while the indefinite a does not. Since the carries more information that a, it will be preferred whenever the presupposition is met (i.e., whenever there is indeed a unique individual matching the NP description in the context). This accounts for the contrast shown in (20), where the indefinite determiner a is infelicitous, despite both (20a) and (20b) being true statements. Instead, the must be used because its presupposition is met: the victim has only one father.

We therefore expect šɛ to be preferred to tə in all PDE contexts, contrary to fact. Instead, tə is used much more frequently than šɛ for PDE contexts, and šɛ shows up sporadically.

form: Why the competition does not play out as expected is a question we cannot fully answer here, but we suggest a possible explanation. Our intuition is that šɛ is not treated as a canonical member of the paradigm, and so the choice between šɛ and the other forms is not based solely on evidential factors. This could be captured if speakers who rarely use šɛ typically use a two-determiner system with tə and kʷ but can switch between this and a three -determiner system that includes šɛ. The choice between these systems would then be stylistic or to do with subtle register factors we have not yet picked up on. If correct, the alternate determiner system actually consists of two paradigms, and some mechanism to switch between them, as schematized in Tables 6 and 7.9 Table 6: Two-determiner system Table 7: Three-determiner system Direct Visual Evidence Evidence Neutral Direct Visual Evidence Evidence Neutral ↔ Current Previous tə kʷ tə šɛ kʷ Above in Section 3.3.4, we speculated that the frequent elision of tə might be due to it being a default determiner used for all entities seen at utterance time and prior. However, the current characterization of the determiner system has kʷ as the least specified and therefore default form. The elision results may instead be more closely tied to frequency effects, with tə being more frequent than kʷ and therefore more easily recovered. This is a matter for future research. The final subtle difference between the paradigms in Tables 4 and 5 concerns whether the core evidential distinction is between direct evidence of all types and evidence neutral or specifically between direct visual evidence and evidence neutral. This is an area that needs further investigation, but here we use the label direct visual evidence to account for the fact that Molly only uses tə for visible entities in the data we have seen so far.

form: In this paper, we document a variant of the ʔayʔaǰuθəm determiner system different to that described in Reisinger et al. (2021). They describe a system with three determiners organized according to evidential distinctions (plus an additional two feminine singular determiners): tə is used when the speaker has direct evidence for the referent at the time of speaking, šɛ is used when the speaker had direct evidence for the referent before the time of speaking, and kʷ is used in all other contexts. For many speakers, however, šɛ is rarely or never used. We examine data from three speakers for whom šɛ does not seem to be a core member of the determiner paradigm. We find that these speakers use tə when referring to entities visible at the time of speaking and previously, while kʷ continues to be used in all other cases, such as where the speaker has only indirect evidence for the referent or talks of things that are hypothetical.

who: Rachel Kelly, Marianne Huijsmans and Mary McCarthy
form: At least two of these speakers do use šɛ occasionally in PDE contexts, despite usually using tə in these cases. We hypothesize that they are able to switch between a three-determiner system and a two-determiner system. The two-determiner system is their default, but they switch to the three- determiner system on occasion, possibly for stylistic reaso ns, although the factors involved still need to be investigated.

The neutral determiners can be used for both visible and invisible referents, while the determiner used for invisible entities is specialized to be used only with invisible entities. form: We hope that this examination of the variation in the determiner system will be helpful for teaching and learning purposes. In laying out both systems, we hope that it will be easier for learners and teachers to understand variation in what they hear from speakers and to determine which system to focus on in different teaching/learning contexts. In particular, learners will likely want to focus on whichever variety they hear from speakers they interact with most often, while teachers will want to be able to guide them in this learning.

who: Rachel Kelly, Marianne Huijsmans and Mary McCarthy
form: This examination also raises a number of interesting linguistic questions, concerning the motivation and trajectory of the changes in the determiner system, as well as how choice between forms plays out in particular contexts. We have speculated that šɛ is in the process of being lost, due to the frequent elision of determiners in everyday speech. However, we have only examined the historical record very cursorily, and future research should involve a more thorough investigation of the determiner system over time.
